Area.evidence_source: Two of the interviewees reflect upon 'having an open door, an option available'; how the thought of being able to put an end to one's suffering if it should become unbearable, is comforting and makes it possible to endure suffering. Another tells of how desperation increased when he was involuntarily hospitalized after the therapist became aware of his suicide plan. Hospitalization restricts access to medications and other methods and also to personal freedom. As one interviewee puts it: There are a few things I just have to keep for myself, well,... and I must have a possibility, I must have an exit which is available. The interviewee explains why he, at the present time, could not tell the staff about his razor blades: 'in a good period, when things work out well for me, when, when I feel I have control over my life, it's in this situation I would be able to see my therapist and talk about this'. An interviewee, who had carried out four suicide attempts in a month, describes the process from the perspective of suicide as relief and consolation to an awareness that suicide was something that could become an actuality: I was never as comfortable as when I first had taken the decision. For about a fortnight or so I just played with the idea, but viewed in retrospect, it wasn't only a play with the idea, but more of a consciousness that I was going to do it in a few weeks. And just that, to lose perspective on what's going to happen, you cannot enjoy anything, everything is just completely indifferent. You play with the thought pretty often (the thought of suicide), and then it's fortified and becomes a kind of obsession, like when you put down a seed that grows and finally overshadows everything, and when the thought is settled, then of course you're afraid to reveal what you've been playing with in your mind... I think it may be difficult for a client to speak up after the thought has changed from being such a comfort, like a dream, to become something like the solution. Freedom and responsibility also entail conflict. The certainty of having control over own life can provide a comfort when suffering feels unbearable. The consolation may change to become an obsession with suicide that overshadows everything and where comfort appears as the solution. Could it be so that the destructive will decide, not the person himself, that I'm doing something I don't want, after all?
